newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury market views G7 meeting as a snoozer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury market views G7 meeting as a snoozer.

text.p: U.S. Treasury market participants plan to keep one eye on this weekend's G7 meeting, but most said they doubt the meeting's outcome will have any effect on the market.
Rather, the market -- already facing a negative tone -- is more focused on upcoming economic news, particularly on labor market data.

"Certainly, if they all came out with a communique that the dollar is too strong, it would have a huge effect," said Larry Dyer, Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "But that is not the likely outcome."

In a worst case scenario, players said the G7 finance ministers and central bankers would collectively deem the dollar too strong, which could send the dollar down and foreigners would sell dollar-denominated assets -- mainly U.S. Treasuries, which would be less attractive.
But that would not bother the market, some participants said.

"If we lose foreign (buying), we'll pick it up from somewhere else," said Vincent Verterano, head government bond trader at Nomura Securities International Inc. "We are starting to pick up buyers from stock guys starting to diversify. Guys I am talking to are not paying attention to (the G7 meeting)," he added. "Guys are worried more if the Fed tightens."

Dyer agreed that the Treasury market is "complacent" about the G7 meeting, but for good reason: Japan's and Europe's economies benefit greatly from a strong dollar, since it helps their export businesses.

Plus, he suggested, talk is cheap. "Unless (foreign central banks) are willing to actively do something, talking (about the dollar being too strong) will not have a significant effect," Dyer said. "If they start to move (via forex intervention) it could have an effect on the Treasury market."

Still, players said that even coordinated intervention would likely be for naught, since the Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates at least by another 50 basis points this year, which stands to further bolster the already strong dollar.
Thursday afternoon, the dollar was trading at 126.25 yen and 1.7160 marks.
The G7 "can say what they want, but the dollar won't weaken much," Verterano said. "They can come out with messages, but they don't control exchange markets."
